question: Can a sparse coordinate encoding coupled to a conventional ResNet-Transformer classifier learn to distinguish prime from composite integers across disjoint contiguous ranges, and what arithmetic structure appears in its false positives?

key_findings.claim: The reported classifier strongly favors recall of primes at the cost of a large composite-to-prime error rate.
key_findings.evidence: For training on integers 0 to 10^6 and testing on 10^6 to 3x10^6, Table 2 reports prime recall 0.9994 but prime precision 0.2704; composite recall is 0.7904, overall accuracy is 0.806, and AUC is 0.895. Thus the headline prime recall does not imply reliable primality decisions.

key_findings.claim: Errors concentrate on composites with few prime factors, especially semiprimes.
key_findings.evidence: The factor-count audit reports that 71.08% of composites with two prime factors are labeled prime, compared with 30.17%, 8.36%, and 1.50% for composites with three, four, and five prime factors. The authors also report that 97.94% of false positives persist across repeated evaluations of the test set.

key_findings.claim: The model reaches its best reported recall after seeing only a small resampled fraction of the training interval, but the experiment does not isolate the sparse encoding from the architecture or the ordered data construction.
key_findings.evidence: With 5% resampling per nominal epoch, Figure 4 places the recall peak around 3,000 to 4,000 iterations, before 5% of the one-million-integer training interval has been presented. Figure 5 reports little performance difference from full-data training over three epochs and describes overfitting in the full-data condition. No dense-encoding, arithmetic-algorithm, or matched-capacity ablation is reported.

key_findings.claim: Performance is reported across several absolute offsets, but the study does not establish algorithmic extrapolation beyond the encoded finite span.
key_findings.evidence: The authors train and test on disjoint ranges around offsets 0, 10^8, and 10^12 and describe similar recall curves; a smaller 0-to-10^5 training interval converges more slowly and overfits. All encodings are nevertheless constrained to a three-million-element span by the fixed 150x150x150 coordinate capacity, and no evaluation changes the span or tests unbounded integer length.

anchors.section: 4.3, variations in training and testing scenarios

method.core_idea: Represent each integer position as a one-hot location in a large sparse four-dimensional tensor, then use a residual feature extractor and Transformer sequence model to predict prime versus composite labels under weighted binary cross-entropy.
method.mechanism: A contiguous sequence of length L is mapped into an L-by-150-by-150-by-150 tensor with one nonzero coordinate per integer, stored as nonzero indices to reduce transfer cost. A ResNet extracts features and a Transformer models dependencies across sequences of normally 15 integers. Training draws a fresh 5% sample of a one-million-integer interval per nominal epoch, upweights primes in the loss, and evaluates recall on a disjoint two-million-integer interval. Additional runs shift the absolute interval or reverse the train/test direction, and false positives are stratified by number of prime factors.
assumptions: A disjoint contiguous integer interval is an informative out-of-distribution test of learned primality rather than primarily a test of interpolation in a fixed positional code.
Prime and composite recall are sufficient primary metrics for an imbalanced task even though the intended decision problem also depends on precision, calibration, and computational cost.
The sparse coordinate uniquely represents the intended integer, including when an absolute offset is used, despite the paper's notation defining coordinates from the sequence index s.
Performance within a fixed three-million-coordinate span is informative about a method whose stated motivation concerns prime numbers more generally.
Conventional primality tests are not needed as efficiency or correctness baselines for the exploratory machine-learning claim.

techniques.role: Maps each integer or sequence position to one active cell in a 150-by-150-by-150 coordinate grid while storing only nonzero indices.
Combines a ResNet feature extractor with a Transformer so individual coordinate features and dependencies among consecutive integers can both influence classification.
Penalizes missed primes more heavily to counter the decreasing density of primes in sequential integer data.
Draws a new small subset of the training interval each nominal epoch to reduce computation and limit repeated exposure.
Groups false positives by the number of prime factors to reveal which composite structures are hardest for the classifier.

evaluations.setting: Train on integers 0 to 10^6; test on the disjoint interval 10^6 to 3x10^6; sequence length 15 and prime class weight 20
evaluations.metric: Per-class precision, recall, F1, overall accuracy, and AUC
evaluations.result: Prime precision/recall/F1 are 0.2704/0.9994/0.4257; composite precision/recall/F1 are 0.9999/0.7904/0.8829; overall accuracy is 0.806 and AUC is 0.895
evaluations.baseline: No deterministic primality-test or non-neural baseline is reported; the table is an absolute performance report

evaluations.setting: Same interval protocol with sequence length and positive-class weight varied
evaluations.result: Weight 3 yields 0% prime recall and 100% composite recall; recall shifts at weight 5 and is described as broadly stable for weights 7 through 25, while sequence length 1 lowers composite recall
evaluations.baseline: Other sequence lengths and class weights within the same architecture

evaluations.setting: Five-percent resampling versus a conventional full-pass training strategy over three epochs
evaluations.result: Recall peaks around 3,000 to 4,000 iterations in the resampled condition, with little plotted difference from full-pass training; the full-pass curve later declines
evaluations.baseline: Training on 100% of the interval per epoch

evaluations.setting: Composite integers from 10^6 to 3x10^6 stratified by number of prime factors
evaluations.result: 71.08% for two factors, 30.17% for three, 8.36% for four, and 1.50% for five
evaluations.baseline: Comparison across arithmetic factor-count strata rather than a competing classifier

evaluations.setting: Disjoint train/test intervals at offsets 0, 10^8, and 10^12, plus reversed high-to-low and reduced-training-range configurations
evaluations.result: The authors describe broadly similar behavior at the larger offsets and in the reversed configuration; training only on 0 to 10^5 converges in roughly 10 to 15 epochs and then overfits
evaluations.baseline: The main 0-to-10^6 training and 10^6-to-3x10^6 testing configuration

limitations: Author-stated: the 150-by-150-by-150 sparse coordinate grid limits every experiment to a span of approximately three million integers because of memory capacity.
Author-stated: prime precision is only 0.2704 and about 20% of composites are falsely labeled prime in the main test, with semiprimes especially difficult.
Author-stated: an epoch means a random 5% subset rather than a conventional full pass, which makes the headline claim of convergence before one epoch easy to misread.

Reviewer-identified: the paper supplies no sieve, Miller-Rabin, deterministic primality test, lookup, Fourier-feature, or simple tabular baseline, so it cannot support a computational advantage claim.

Reviewer-identified: the absolute integer, within-sequence position, and offset semantics of the encoding are underspecified; the equations map s itself to coordinates and leave unclear how offset-shifted integers remain distinguishable.

Reviewer-identified: train/test data are contiguous ordered integers, and there are no random held-out residues, adversarial pseudoprimes, larger coordinate spans, or length extrapolation tests that would separate algorithm learning from finite-domain regularities.

Post-publication status: the current arXiv record states that the work was withdrawn after further analysis found the proposed direction did not lead to meaningful or valid conclusions; the cached source reviewed here is the still-available official v1 PDF.
failure_modes: Class weighting can obtain near-perfect prime recall by shifting the threshold toward predicting prime, while poor prime precision makes the classifier unsuitable as a primality oracle.
A positional one-hot code can encourage memorization or finite-range interpolation rather than a reusable divisibility algorithm.
A model may exploit the local density of primes or correlations among neighboring sequence elements and fail on randomly permuted integers or distant scales.
Semiprimes and other composites with few factors resemble primes under weak learned heuristics, producing the observed concentrated false-positive pattern.
The fixed coordinate grid grows with the represented integer span, so memory cost can dominate well before the method approaches cryptographically relevant integers.
Ambiguous offset handling can silently make nominally different absolute ranges share the same encoded positions, invalidating an extrapolation interpretation.
reusable_insights: For imbalanced algorithmic classification, report precision-recall tradeoffs and false-positive structure rather than highlighting only recall on the rare class.
Stratifying errors by mathematically meaningful hardness variables, such as factor count or smallest factor, can reveal the heuristic a model has learned.
A claim that a network learned an algorithm needs tests that expand input length or numeric range without expanding a lookup-like representation.
Encoding ablations should compare positional one-hot, digit, residue, Fourier, and raw scalar features at matched capacity and compute.
Withdrawal metadata is substantive evidence: downstream research ideas should treat the empirical direction as a cautionary test case, not a positive result awaiting scale.
open_questions: Does the reported model beat a constant-threshold classifier at matched prime recall once precision-recall curves are compared over the full test interval?
What information about the absolute integer survives the sparse encoding when training and test intervals use nonzero offsets?
Would performance persist on uniformly sampled integers, pseudoprimes, products of two large primes, and spans far larger than the training coordinate grid?
Which result or analysis motivated the authors' later withdrawal, and can an independently reproduced pipeline identify the exact invalidating mechanism?
Can a compact minimum-description network discover a genuine primality program from examples without a representation whose size scales linearly with the finite domain?

competitive_landscape.title: Classification of integers based on residue classes via modern deep learning algorithms
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct prior task and feature-engineering control
competitive_landscape.difference: Wu et al. classify residues modulo small integers and show that feature space, rather than deeper CNN/RNN/Transformer architectures, controls success; their Fourier-basis linear regression reaches exact residue classification, providing the kind of interpretable arithmetic baseline missing from the primality study.

competitive_landscape.title: Integer Factorisation, Fermat & Machine Learning on a Classical Computer
competitive_landscape.difference: Blake reduces Fermat-style factorization to a binary classification problem and synthetically generates prime-derived training data, but explicitly frames the experiments as falling short of a practical scalable factorization algorithm; it targets useful factors rather than high recall on bounded primality labels.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Networks Generalize on Low Complexity Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Chatterjee and Sudijono prove that a minimum-description-length ReLU interpolator can generalize on primality sampled uniformly from 1 to N because primality has a short program; this is a theoretical existence result tied to description length, not evidence that an ordinary sparsely encoded trained network discovers that program.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a novel highly sparse encoding integrated with conventional neural networks for prime/composite classification, rapid convergence, and a factor-structured analysis of persistent false positives.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The v1 experiments provide per-class metrics over several finite contiguous ranges and stratify composite errors by prime-factor count, but do not include encoding ablations, arithmetic baselines, scaling tests, or uncertainty estimates.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The most defensible novelty is the finite-range error audit showing that semiprimes dominate false positives. The broader suggestion that the system learns a meaningful prime-number model is not supported and is further undermined by the authors' later withdrawal notice stating that the direction did not yield meaningful or valid conclusions.

reviewer_notes: The primary reading used the official versioned v1 PDF because the unversioned arXiv PDF is unavailable after withdrawal. Quantitative statements are author-reported unless labeled reviewer-identified. Competitor titles, abstracts, and versions were checked on their primary arXiv records on 2026-08-23. The withdrawal statement comes from the current primary arXiv metadata, not from the v1 PDF, and materially lowers confidence in causal or scaling interpretations.
